positions/existentialist-theology/oneLin: The gospel addresses the human situation of anxiety, guilt and finitude; its mythological language must be interpreted existentially so that it calls modern people to authentic existence and faith.
positions/existentialist-theology/coreCl: The New Testament world-picture is mythological; its kerygma must be demythologised, not discarded (Bultmann).
Faith is a decision to live from God’s future rather than from one’s own securities.
Theology correlates existential questions with the answers of revelation (Tillich).
God is not a being among others but being-itself, the ground of being; faith is ultimate concern.
positions/existentialist-theology/keyTex: Tillich, Systematic Theology; The Courage to Be (1952)
positions/existentialist-theology/origin: Drawing on Kierkegaard and Heidegger, Rudolf Bultmann’s 1941 lecture launched the demythologising programme, and Paul Tillich in America built a philosophical theology of correlation. Both had roots in the dialectical revolt against liberalism but moved in different directions from Barth.
positions/existentialist-theology/strong: It made the New Testament speak to modern people without demanding a pre-scientific worldview.
It takes seriously anxiety, meaninglessness and the search for authenticity.
It connected theology with philosophy, psychology and culture.
Barth and others said it turned theology into anthropology and lost the objectivity of God’s acts.
Conservatives objected that it dissolved the bodily resurrection and the historical basis of faith.
Later critics found existentialism individualistic and blind to social and political structures (Moltmann, liberation theology).
positions/existentialist-theology/respon: Bultmann insisted the kerygma’s "that" (Christ crucified as God’s act) remains; Tillich held that symbols participate in what they point to.
positions/existentialist-theology/conseq: The "new quest" of the historical Jesus.
Death-of-God and radical theologies of the 1960s; pastoral theology influenced by psychology.
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/oneLin: Orthodox theology must free itself from Western scholastic and idealist "captivity" and acquire the mind of the Fathers, rethinking their vision creatively for today, with apophaticism, deification and the essence-energies distinction at its centre.
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/coreCl: The Fathers are not a past epoch but a living norm: theology must think in their spirit (Christian Hellenism).
Doctrine and mystical experience are inseparable.
God is known apophatically and participated through uncreated energies, aiming at theosis.
Orthodox theology since the 17th century had been distorted by Latin and Protestant borrowings ("pseudomorphosis").
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/keyTex: Lossky, Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church (1944)
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/origin: Proclaimed by Georges Florovsky at the first Congress of Orthodox Theology at Athens (1936) and developed in the Russian emigration in Paris (Lossky, Meyendorff, Schmemann) and in Romania (Stăniloae) and Greece (Romanides, Yannaras, Zizioulas). It largely displaced the Russian religious philosophy of Soloviev and Bulgakov.
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/strong: It recovered the patristic and Byzantine heritage, including Palamas, for modern Orthodoxy and the West.
It gave Orthodoxy a confident voice in the ecumenical movement.
It united dogma, liturgy and spirituality.
Critics (e.g. sophiologists, some recent Orthodox scholars) say it constructed an anti-Western identity and caricatured Western theology.
Its notion of a single "mind of the Fathers" can flatten patristic diversity.
Western critics question the essence-energies distinction itself.
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/respon: Advocates acknowledge polemical excesses but argue the core recovery of the Fathers stands; Florovsky himself was a committed ecumenist.
positions/neo-patristic-synthesis/conseq: Shaped Orthodox seminaries (St Vladimir’s, St Sergius) and ecumenical dialogue.
Western rediscovery of theosis and Palamas.
positions/nouvelle-theologie/oneLine: Catholic theology should be renewed not by abstract neo-scholastic manuals but by a return to the sources: Scripture, the Fathers, the liturgy and the authentic Aquinas, read historically and in dialogue with modern life.
positions/nouvelle-theologie/coreClaims/: Theology is historical: doctrines must be understood in their development and original contexts.
Nature is oriented to God by a natural desire for the supernatural; there is no sealed-off "pure nature".
The Church is the body of Christ formed by the Eucharist, a sacrament of communion for all humanity.
Renewal (aggiornamento) comes through return to the sources (ressourcement).
positions/nouvelle-theologie/keyTexts/2: Congar, True and False Reform in the Church (1950)
positions/nouvelle-theologie/origin: Emerged among French Jesuits at Lyon-Fourvière (de Lubac, Daniélou) and Dominicans at Le Saulchoir (Chenu, Congar) in the 1930s-40s; the label was coined by its critic Réginald Garrigou-Lagrange in 1946. Censured indirectly by Humani Generis (1950), its leaders became architects of Vatican II.
positions/nouvelle-theologie/strongestAr: It reconnected theology with Scripture, the Fathers, liturgy and spirituality.
It shaped Vatican II’s constitutions on revelation and the Church.
It opened Catholicism to ecumenical and Orthodox dialogue.
positions/nouvelle-theologie/strongestOb: Neo-Thomists charged it with historical relativism and with compromising the gratuity of grace.
Some later critics argue that it weakened doctrinal clarity after the Council.
Progressives in turn found its later representatives (Balthasar, Ratzinger) too conservative.
positions/nouvelle-theologie/responses/0: Ressourcement theologians insisted they were faithful to Aquinas read in context and that return to sources serves tradition.
positions/nouvelle-theologie/consequence: Vatican II documents Dei Verbum and Lumen Gentium.
Communio school (Balthasar, Ratzinger) and Sources Chrétiennes series.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/oneLine: Secular reason is not neutral but a heretical theology in disguise; Christianity should recover a participatory, Platonic-Augustinian ontology in which all reality shares in God, and out-narrate modernity.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/coreClaims/0: Every account of reality is implicitly theological; there is no neutral secular ground.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/coreClaims/1: Creation participates in God; the late-medieval turn to univocity and nominalism severed this and produced modernity.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/coreClaims/2: The Church’s liturgy and community embody an ontology of peace against the ontology of violence.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/coreClaims/3: Theology may speak about every field: politics, economics, aesthetics, science.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/keyTexts/3: Milbank, Pickstock and Ward (eds.), Radical Orthodoxy (1999)
positions/radical-orthodoxy/origin: Launched at Cambridge by John Milbank’s Theology and Social Theory (1990) and the collection Radical Orthodoxy (1999) with Catherine Pickstock and Graham Ward, drawing on Augustine, Aquinas, de Lubac and postmodern philosophy.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/strongestArg: It exposes hidden assumptions in secular social theory.
It recovers a sacramental vision of creation shared with patristic and Orthodox theology.
It energised Christian engagement with philosophy and politics.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/strongestObj: Historians dispute its genealogy blaming Scotus and Ockham for modernity.
Critics find it triumphalist, idealised about the Church and weak on Scripture.
Protestants question its sacramental ontology; others its dense, polemical style.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/responses/0: Proponents say the genealogy is a theological narrative, not a mere history, and that idealising the Church is a call to repentance.
positions/radical-orthodoxy/consequences: Influenced political theology and debates on secularism.
Revived interest in participation and Christian Platonism.
positions/postliberal-theology/oneLine: Christianity is like a language and culture: doctrine is the grammar of a community whose identity is formed by the biblical story, so the Church should absorb the world into the text rather than translate the text into the world’s terms.
positions/postliberal-theology/coreClaim: Religions are cultural-linguistic systems that shape experience, rather than expressions of a prior universal experience.
Doctrines function as rules for speech and practice.
Scripture is read as a realistic narrative identifying Jesus Christ (Frei); intratextuality.
The Church is a distinct community whose faithfulness is its social ethic (Hauerwas).
positions/postliberal-theology/keyTexts/: Frei, The Eclipse of Biblical Narrative (1974)
positions/postliberal-theology/origin: Developed at Yale by George Lindbeck and Hans Frei, building on Barth and Wittgenstein; popularised by Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon (Resident Aliens, 1989).
positions/postliberal-theology/strongest: It frees theology from having to justify itself by liberal or rationalist criteria.
It recovers the Bible’s narrative shape and the formative role of the Church.
It offered an ecumenical model for doctrinal reconciliation.
Evangelicals and Catholics asked whether it weakens doctrine’s claim to be true about reality (Carl Henry’s critique of Frei).
Liberals charged it with fideism and sectarian withdrawal.
Others question its idealised picture of church communities.
positions/postliberal-theology/responses: Postliberals answer that doctrine can be true when used rightly within practice and that witness, not withdrawal, is intended.
positions/postliberal-theology/consequen: Influenced theological interpretation of Scripture and ecclesial ethics.
Shaped ecumenical dialogue and some evangelical theology.
positions/black-theology/oneLine: God reveals himself in Jesus as the liberator of the oppressed; in a society structured by white racism, the gospel is good news of Black liberation and theology must speak from the Black experience.
positions/black-theology/coreClaims/0: The Exodus and Jesus’ ministry to the poor show that God sides with the oppressed.
positions/black-theology/coreClaims/1: Black experience, history and culture (spirituals, blues, sermons) are sources of theology.
positions/black-theology/coreClaims/2: White theology has often served racism and must be confronted.
positions/black-theology/coreClaims/3: Christ is "Black" in that he identifies with the suffering and struggle of Black people.
positions/black-theology/keyTexts/3: Cone, Black Theology and Black Power (1969)
positions/black-theology/origin: Emerged in the United States in 1969 with James Cone amid the civil rights and Black Power movements (the National Committee of Black Churchmen) and in South Africa in the early 1970s within the Black Consciousness movement (Allan Boesak, Manas Buthelezi), feeding the struggle against apartheid.
positions/black-theology/strongestArgume: It speaks from the long experience of Black churches and their faith under slavery and segregation.
It recovers the Bible’s concern for justice and the poor.
It exposed the complicity of much theology with racism and apartheid.
positions/black-theology/strongestObject: Some critics said it subordinates the gospel to a political programme or racial identity.
J. Deotis Roberts and others urged more emphasis on reconciliation; womanists criticised its early neglect of gender.
Conservative critics question its use of experience as a norm alongside Scripture.
positions/black-theology/responses/0: Cone replied that there is no reconciliation without liberation, and that all theology is contextual, white theology included.
positions/black-theology/consequences/0: Influenced the Kairos Document (1985) and anti-apartheid theology.
positions/black-theology/consequences/1: Black church studies and womanist theology.
